opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think physical intelligence is a really fundamental part of intelligence, and in some ways it's the part we've historically underestimated. There's this classic observation, Moravec's paradox, that the things that feel hard to us, like playing chess or doing calculus, have turned out to be relatively easy for machines, while the things that feel effortless, like picking up a cup, folding a shirt, or walking across a cluttered room, have been incredibly hard. That tells you that a huge amount of intelligence is wrapped up in how we perceive and act in the physical world. We just don't notice it because evolution spent so long refining it.

When I think about where it fits more broadly, I see it as both a capability in its own right and something that grounds other kinds of intelligence. Language models have learned an enormous amount from text, and they know a lot *about* the world, but there's a difference between knowing that a towel is soft and deformable and actually being able to fold one. That second kind of knowledge, the knowledge you get through interaction, through feedback from your own actions, is something you can really only get by being embodied, or by learning from data that comes from embodied experience.

I'm also excited about the convergence happening right now. A few years ago robotics and the rest of machine learning felt pretty separate. Now we're seeing that a lot of the same recipes, large models, diverse data, pretraining and then fine-tuning, can transfer to robotics, and that we can build on vision-language models as a foundation for robot policies. So I don't see physical intelligence as a separate track. I see it as part of the same broader effort, where the goal is systems that can understand the world and act in it flexibly, across many tasks and many environments, rather than being engineered for one narrow thing.

And practically, if we want AI to have a big impact on people's everyday lives, so much of what matters happens in the physical world: in homes, in hospitals, in warehouses, in manufacturing. Getting intelligence out of the screen and into the world is, to me, one of the most important and most interesting open problems we have.

r001.rationale: It says physical intelligence has historically been underestimated and explains that seemingly effortless actions like picking up a cup or walking require substantial intelligence.

r002.rationale: It calls physical intelligence a fundamental part of intelligence and says it both stands as a capability and grounds other kinds of intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot. My view is that physical intelligence is really core to intelligence more broadly, and in some ways it's actually the harder part. If you look at how intelligence evolved in humans and animals, it didn't start with language or abstract reasoning. It started with being able to move around in the world, perceive it, manipulate things, and accomplish goals physically. Language and higher-level reasoning came much, much later, and they were built on top of that foundation.

And what's been interesting about the trajectory of AI is that it's gone almost in the opposite order. We've gotten systems that can write code and pass exams and have really fluent conversations, and yet we still don't have a robot that can reliably clean up a kitchen or fold laundry in a home it's never seen before. That's Moravec's paradox, and it's held up remarkably well. The things that are easy for a toddler are still really hard for machines.

Part of why that is comes down to data. Language models could ride on the entire internet, which is this enormous byproduct of humans doing things online. There's no equivalent corpus of robots acting in the physical world. We've had to build that from scratch, through teleoperation, through scaling up data collection across many robots and many environments. So the bottleneck has been less about ideas and more about actually getting the experience into the system.

But I don't think of physical intelligence as a separate thing you bolt onto an AI system at the end. I think of it as a test of whether a model really understands the world. When a robot has to pick something up, it has to deal with physics, with uncertainty, with the fact that its actions have consequences and it can't just regenerate a response. There's a feedback loop with reality that's very grounding. And I think a lot of the common-sense understanding that we want from intelligent systems generally, things like what happens if I push this, how heavy is that, what's going to break, is most naturally learned through that kind of interaction.

What's exciting right now is that these threads are starting to merge. You can take the semantic and visual knowledge from large pretrained models and combine it with robot data, and you get systems that generalize in ways that would've seemed out of reach a few years ago. So my hope is that physical intelligence stops being this niche corner of the field and becomes part of the same story. If we want AI that's genuinely useful in people's lives, not just on screens, it has to be able to act in the world, and I think solving that will also make our models smarter in a more general sense.

r001.rationale: The response says physical intelligence is harder and that tasks easy for toddlers remain difficult for machines, but it does not state that people underestimate the intelligence motor control requires.

r002.rationale: The response explicitly describes physical intelligence as “really core to intelligence more broadly” and as a foundation for higher-level reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think physical intelligence is a pretty fundamental part of intelligence more broadly. If you look at humans, a lot of what we learn comes from interacting with the world. We move things around, we try things, we see what happens, and that gives us an understanding of cause and effect that’s hard to get just from observing.

And what’s interesting is that things we find effortless—picking up a glass, putting on a jacket, walking through a cluttered room—are still really challenging for robots. They require perception, reasoning, and control to work together, with feedback coming in continuously. You can’t just decide on a plan and assume everything will happen exactly as you expected.

So I see embodiment as both an important capability in its own right and a way to study intelligence. Can a system learn from its own experience? Can it adapt when something unexpected happens? Can it take what it learned in one situation and apply it in another? Those questions matter well beyond robotics, but the physical world gives us a very concrete way to test them.

r001.rationale: The response says familiar actions feel effortless to people yet remain difficult for robots, but it does not state that people underestimate the intelligence motor control requires.

r002.rationale: It describes physical intelligence as a “pretty fundamental part of intelligence more broadly,” directly communicating that it is central.

sol-6.1.text:
I think embodied intelligence is a really important part of intelligence more broadly. If you look at how humans learn, a lot of it comes from interacting with the world. We take actions, observe what happens, and build an understanding of what we can control and how things work.

And that’s a somewhat different setting from learning from a fixed dataset. When you’re interacting with the world, your actions determine the data you get next. You can try something to test a hypothesis, or move an object to see what’s behind it. So intelligence is partly about making predictions, but it’s also about choosing actions that help you learn and accomplish things.

I don’t think that means every intelligent system needs a physical body. But I do think that if we want systems that can help us with the full range of things people do, they’ll need some way to understand and interact with the physical world. Robotics is a really compelling way to study that, because the world gives you very concrete feedback about whether your understanding is actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning through interaction and taking actions, but does not say people underestimate the intelligence motor control requires.

r002.rationale: It calls embodied intelligence “a really important part of intelligence more broadly” and explains its role in learning and interacting with the physical world.
